analysis.one_liner: Adds hearings, cost tests, and court review that make major federal regulations slower and easier to challenge.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and never received a committee vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the basic procedures federal agencies must follow when writing major rules — the rules that carry out laws on clean air and water, workplace safety, food and drug safety, and consumer finance. It would require agencies to hold formal trial-like hearings, with cross-examination and the burden of proof on the government, for the biggest rules; to adopt the option that 'maximizes net benefits' — generally the least costly one — unless a White House office approves otherwise; and to make it easier for regulated parties to challenge rules in court. It died in committee without a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and trade associations that face major federal regulations. They gain new tools to stall and challenge rules on their profits: a right to petition for formal hearings where the agency must prove its case, a mandate that agencies pick the cheapest compliant option, broader grounds for lawsuits, and a requirement that agencies consider simply rescinding existing rules instead of writing new ones.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing major federal rules

how_it_helps.text: For 'high-impact' rules (roughly $500 million or more a year in economic effect), any interested party could petition for a public hearing with oral presentation, cross-examination, and the burden of proof on the agency proposing the rule — a formal process that can take months or years and stalls a rule while disputes play out.

For major and high-impact rules, the agency would have to adopt the alternative that maximizes net benefits — in practice the lowest-cost option — and could only choose a costlier rule if the White House regulatory office approved and the agency documented why unquantified benefits justified it.

The bill widens the scope of judicial review, letting courts send a rule back to an agency without striking it down, and requires judges to check whether the agency's factual findings are supported by 'substantial evidence' for high-impact rules — giving regulated companies more ways to keep a rule tied up in court.

Agencies would be barred from publicly encouraging comment on their own proposed rules in anything but an 'impartial manner' — meaning the government could not make the public case for its own protections, while affected companies remain free to lobby against them.

Supporters' case, in their own terms: agencies would have to publish the data behind a rule, consider a reasonable number of alternatives including market-based and disclosure approaches, and periodically assess whether major rules are working — cost discipline and transparency for rules that can cost $100 million or more a year.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal protections — from clean air and water to workplace safety, food and drug safety, and fair treatment by banks and debt collectors. Slower and easier-to-block rulemaking means known hazards stay unaddressed longer, and weakened standards leave the cost of harm on individuals rather than the companies causing it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The formal hearing process for high-impact rules puts the burden of proof on the agency and allows cross-examination over 'genuinely disputed' factual issues — an opening that regulated parties can use to stall any large rule on public health, safety, or financial protection while the underlying hazard continues.

Requiring agencies to adopt the rule that maximizes net benefits can block protections whose benefits are real but hard to put a dollar figure on — such as avoided deaths or illness — unless a White House office signs off on the exception.

An honest supporter's cost: the added hearings, expanded comment periods, documentation, and litigation exposure would delay virtually every major rule, including ones with broad support, and the bill does not fund agencies to absorb the extra workload.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and retrospective-review pieces have real value, and cost accountability for hundred-million-dollar rules is a fair goal. But the bill's core mechanics — trial-like hearings where the agency bears the burden of proof, a default to the cheapest option, and broader court challenges — are built to slow and shrink the rules that carry out environmental, workplace, food, drug, and financial-protection laws. For a bill with no cosponsors and no committee action, the trade was never tested in public.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors, read twice, and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rob Portman introduced the bill on January 16, 2020; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day.
No cosponsor ever signed on — the cosponsor list shows zero for the entire Congress.
The action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote; the bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead of where they would have been under the bill: the existing rulemaking process and the protections that flow through it remained intact. No industry gained anything from this bill's fate beyond avoiding a change it likely wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing federal protections stayed in place

sides.party_line_note: A Republican introduced the bill, not a single senator of either party cosponsored it, and it never came to a vote, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, chemicals, finance, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals)
industries.note: The bill would give any regulated company new levers — formal hearings with cross-examination, a cheapest-option mandate, and broader lawsuits — to delay or dilute major rules on air, water, workplaces, drugs, and consumer finance. The savings show up as fewer compliance costs; the exposure shows up as weaker protections for the public.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and the White House regulatory review office (OIRA)
industries.note: The bill would substantially expand OIRA's power, requiring agencies to clear proposed and final major rules with the Administrator and routing exceptions to the cost mandate through that office, while saddling agencies with hearing, documentation, and assessment duties without new funding. Power concentrates in one White House office; workloads and delay rise across the government.
